# Tools for AI Agents: MCP and Durable Writes

A language-model assistant that can read and write files on a person's
behalf needs some way to reach those files. Giving it a shell, or a
database connection, or the person's credentials, hands it far more than it
needs. The Model Context Protocol exists to give it exactly a set of named
tools with typed arguments and nothing else. This chapter describes the
FOKS MCP server, which lets an assistant read and write an encrypted
key-value store, and the idempotency mechanism that makes its writes safe
to retry.

## The Model Context Protocol in brief

The *Model Context Protocol* (MCP) is an open specification for connecting
assistants to external capabilities. A *server* exposes tools (functions
the model may call), resources (data it may read), and prompts; a *client*,
usually embedded in the assistant's host application, discovers those and
invokes them. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0, a small remote-procedure-call
format in which a request has an `id`, a `method`, and `params`, and a
response carries the same `id` with either a `result` or an `error`. The
transport FOKS uses is *stdio*: the client spawns the server as a child
process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON over its standard input and
output. No network port is opened.

A tool call is `tools/call` with a tool name and a JSON object of
arguments; the reply carries content blocks (text, here) and optionally
*structured content*, a JSON object the client can act on without parsing
prose.

## The FOKS tool sets

The server is started from the command-line tool:

```
foks-rs --state-dir DIR mcp kv   --profile P --account-alias A [--read-only]
foks-rs --state-dir DIR mcp team --profile P --account-alias A
```

It binds one profile, one account, and one authenticated host for the life
of the process. Two tool sets exist.

| Set | Tools |
|---|---|
| Team | `list`, `list-memberships` |
| KV, read-only | `list`, `get`, `stat`, `usage` |
| KV, normal | the four above plus `put`, `mkdir`, `rm`, `mv`, `foks_status`, `foks_pending` |

The ten upstream tool names and their behaviors are compared against
go-foks v0.1.9 by a compatibility script that drives both the Rust and the
pinned Go services through an independent Go MCP SDK. `foks_status` and
`foks_pending` are local recovery additions with no upstream counterpart.
(The repository's HTML guide calls these `fennec_status` and
`fennec_pending` and places `usage` in the Team set; the code uses the
`foks_` prefix and puts `usage` in the KV set. The code is authoritative.)

Paths refer to the encrypted namespace of [Chapter 14](14-kv-store.qmd);
symlinks are resolved inside that namespace with a 32-hop limit and cycle
detection. Binary content travels as standard base64. A `team` argument
selects an accessible team, which the server resolves through the agent and
re-checks to be the same profile, account, host, and user; it cannot select
another account or state directory.

Arguments deserialize with `deny_unknown_fields`, so a misspelled or extra
key is an error rather than silently ignored. The `put` arguments zeroize
their content on drop, the invocation type deliberately does not implement
`Debug` because content can contain credentials, and deserialization errors
are never echoed to the caller because they can quote input.

### Read-only mode

`--read-only` omits every write tool from the advertised list and rejects
calls to them. It is the mode to use when the assistant's job is to consult
secrets rather than change them, and it makes the reduction visible to the
client at `tools/list` time instead of at first failure.

## Bounds

| Bound | Value |
|---|---|
| Input frame | 8 MiB |
| Output frame | 8 MiB (checked on the *encoded* JSON, minus 1 KiB for the envelope) |
| Decoded file content | 4 MiB |
| Catalog or roster rows per page | 1,000 |
| Active calls | 4 |
| Queued calls | 16 |
| Stalled stdout timeout | 30 s |

Concurrency is a semaphore of four permits; each backend call runs on a
blocking thread with the permit held, and cancellation of the JSON-RPC
request is linked to a child cancellation token so that dropping the
request interrupts the blocking IPC read. The output size is checked on the
serialized bytes rather than the plaintext length because JSON escaping can
expand a string as much as sixfold. The transport keeps a per-request-ID
"publishing" marker while a response is being flushed, so a client that
reuses an ID immediately after seeing the response bytes waits for the
flush to complete, and a 30-second stall timeout ensures a blocked stdout
cannot wedge the process.

## No authentication at the MCP layer, and why

The server does not authenticate its client. There is no token, no
password prompt, and no PIN entry on stdin. That is a deliberate choice,
and the boundary it relies on is the local socket.

The MCP process runs as the local user and connects to that user's own
`foks-rs.sock`. The agent on the other end accepts a connection only if the
peer's UID, obtained from the kernel via `SO_PEERCRED` or `LOCAL_PEERCRED`,
equals its own ([Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd)); the socket file is mode 0600
and owner-checked on the client side too. Anyone who can spawn the MCP
process can already read the same socket directly, so an MCP-level secret
would add a step without adding a boundary. The account must already be
usable by the agent (initialized, provisioned, and unlocked through the
ordinary client); MCP never asks for the credentials that would make it
so. If the agent is not running, the CLI starts the packaged sibling
executable found next to itself, never a shell command or an executable
named by a tool call.

## Idempotency keys

An assistant that calls `put` and then loses the connection before the
reply has a problem: did the write happen? Calling `put` again might
create a duplicate or overwrite a concurrent change; not calling it might
leave the work undone. The general remedy, familiar from payment APIs, is
the *idempotency key*: the caller attaches a unique identifier to a
request, the server records the outcome under that identifier, and a
repeated request with the same identifier returns the recorded outcome
rather than executing again. Stripe popularized the pattern, and an IETF
draft standardizes an `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header for it.

Two details make the pattern sound. The key must be bound to the request's
content, so that reusing a key with different inputs is rejected rather
than answered with the earlier result. And the server must record the key
*before* it acts, so that a crash between acting and recording cannot
produce a second execution.

## Durable submission IDs

Every FOKS MCP write carries a *submission ID* with this canonical form:

```
v1-<16 lowercase hex Unix seconds>-<32 lowercase hex random>
```

That is a version tag, an issuance time, and 128 random bits, 52 characters
in all. The server generates one for each write by default. A client may
instead supply its own, which is how an assistant keeps its intent across a
restart of the MCP process: it records the ID before calling, and if the
reply is lost it asks after the same ID rather than issuing a new write.
Reusing an ID with different inputs, including a different team, is
rejected; the ledger stores a hash of the inputs alongside the ID for
exactly this comparison. A JSON-RPC request ID is not a submission ID and
is never used as one.

Every write's structured result carries four fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `submission_id` | the ID under which this write is recorded |
| `status` | `prepared`, `committed`, `rejected`, or `unknown` |
| `partial` | ancillary namespace work committed but final completion is unproven |
| `node_id` | the resulting node, present only when authenticated evidence proves it |

The status words have precise meanings. *Prepared* means remote delivery
has not begun; the same input under the same ID may execute once. *Committed*
means the operation has sufficient acknowledgment or exact namespace
evidence. *Rejected* means it cannot execute under that ID. *Unknown* means
delivery may have occurred: the assistant must inspect status instead of
issuing the write with a new ID.

The two recovery tools serve that inspection. `foks_status` takes a
submission ID and reads or reconciles the recorded intent, which may
involve the agent re-reading the directory to find out whether the write
landed ([Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd) covers that reconciliation).
`foks_pending` lists intents that are pending, including handles whose
original preparation or result reply was lost, so an assistant that has
forgotten what it was doing can find out.

### Exactly-once under retries

The guarantee these pieces add up to is *exactly-once* from the caller's
point of view, under the discipline that a caller never repeats a mutation
with a new ID after an unknown outcome. The submission ledger lives in the
agent's hard-state database, where its rows are protected by triggers: the
identifying fields of a submission are immutable once written, a user is
capped at 64 active and 65,536 retained intents, and terminal evidence is
retained for 30 days before it may be pruned. Pending and uncertain
submissions are never deleted by age or storage pressure, because deleting
one would turn "unknown" into "forgotten."

The ledger also has a clock discipline. New handles must be no more than 24
hours old and no more than five minutes in the future; a durable rejection
watermark, made irreversible by a trigger, prevents a clock set backward
from reopening handles that were already refused as stale. A wall-clock
jump of more than five minutes, or a restart more than 24 hours past the
last trusted floor, blocks new admission with `clock-untrusted` while status
and recovery continue to work; an operator repairs the anchor with an
explicit two-step command.

Cancellation is honored but does not undo remote work; a cancelled request
answers "check mutation status before retrying." An interrupted upload may
leave an unreferenced encrypted object on the server, which the server's
bounded reclamation ([Chapter 18](18-server-storage.qmd)) collects later. A
lost delete acknowledgment can remain unknown indefinitely, because the
current absence of a name cannot prove which delete removed it.

## Protocol versions

The server advertises MCP revision 2025-11-25 and negotiates 2025-06-18,
2025-03-26, and 2024-11-05 through the official Rust SDK, pinned to an
exact version. Advertising the newest and accepting older revisions lets
an assistant host that has not yet updated continue to work.

The local agent IPC is separate: its current version is 31. Upgrade the CLI
and resident agent together and restart the agent to avoid a version mismatch.
The hard-state database uses schema 40 and migrates supported schemas 38 and
39; other development schemas are refused. These upgrades do not turn an
unknown mutation outcome into permission to replay it.

## Where to look

- `foks-mcp`: `contract.rs` (limits, tool sets, argument types),
  `session.rs` (concurrency, cancellation, output bound, protocol
  versions), `transport.rs` (stdio codec, publishing marker, stall
  timeout), `agent.rs` and `agent/writes.rs` (scope binding, path
  resolution, submission handles), `README.md`.
- `foks-cli`: `mcp.rs` (entry point, `ensure_agent`).
- `foks-proto`: `submission.rs` (`SubmissionHandle`).
- `foks-client-db`: the `kv_adapter_submissions` and `kv_adapter_clocks`
  tables in `schema.rs`, `repositories/adapter/`.
- `tools/foks-v019-oracle/run-mcp-compat.sh`.
